title: How do you get medicines in the UK? Prescriptions, Pharmacy First, and the medicines you took back home
summary: Prescriptions and pharmacy services in England, prescription charges and exemptions, and what to check if you take medicine prescribed abroad.
content:
# How do you get medicines in the UK? Prescriptions, Pharmacy First, and the medicines you took back home

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own rules on prescription charges and what pharmacies can do, which differ from England; we will cover them separately.

In England, getting medicines may work differently from what you are used to. There are roughly three ways to get them: some can be bought in supermarkets, some only in a pharmacy with a pharmacist present, and some need a prescription. Once you know which group the medicine you need is in, a lot becomes simpler.

## Three groups of medicines: supermarket, pharmacy, prescription

The UK puts medicines into three groups:

- **General Sales List (GSL)**: available in supermarkets and corner shops, and from pharmacy shelves without asking;
- **Pharmacy medicines (P)**: only sold in a pharmacy, with a pharmacist present;
- **Prescription only medicines (POM)**: need a prescription from a doctor or another health professional who is allowed to prescribe, collected from a pharmacy. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-three-medicine-classes)

So if you can't find a medicine in the supermarket, it does not necessarily mean the UK doesn't have it; you may need to ask at a pharmacy, or you may need a prescription.

## If you feel unwell, you can start at a pharmacy

In England, a pharmacy is not just a shop for medicines. The pharmacist can look at your situation, give advice, and tell you what to buy or who to see.

Since the end of January 2024, England has had an NHS service called **Pharmacy First**. For the seven conditions below, you can go straight to a pharmacy, without first booking a GP appointment or being referred:

- sinusitis: aged 12 and over;
- sore throat: aged 5 and over;
- acute otitis media (middle ear infection): aged 1 to 17;
- infected insect bite: aged 1 and over;
- impetigo: aged 1 and over;
- shingles: aged 18 and over;
- uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI): women aged 16 to 64. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-first-seven-conditions)

The pharmacist will follow a set clinical pathway, give you self-care advice, and only when appropriate supply a medicine from a small, restricted set of prescription medicines. In other words, you may not be given medicine, and pharmacists cannot deal with every minor illness. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-first-pathway-limits)

For problems outside this range, the pharmacist may suggest you see a GP or use another service. This is the normal division of work, not being brushed off. Before you go, you can phone to check whether that pharmacy offers Pharmacy First. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-first-pathway-limits)

GP practices and NHS 111 may also send you to a pharmacy for some minor illnesses. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-pharmacy-first-pathway-limits)

## How prescriptions work, and how much they cost

Once a GP or another health professional who is allowed to prescribe gives you a prescription, you collect the medicine from a pharmacy.

In England, prescriptions are charged **per item**, not per prescription. For 2026/27 the charge is **£9.90 per item**, the same as the previous year. If one prescription has three medicines on it, you pay £9.90 three times. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-charge-per-item)

Some prescribed items are always free, such as contraception and medicines for hospital inpatients. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-charge-per-item)

## Who gets free prescriptions?

Some people in England get free prescriptions, depending on age, pregnancy or having recently had a baby, certain medical conditions, and whether they receive certain benefits or have a low income. The conditions are detailed, so the most reliable way is to use the eligibility checker on the website of NHSBSA (the organisation that handles help with NHS costs). [See the official source](#guide-evidence-free-prescription-eligibility)

Two points can be made clear now:

- **Paying the IHS does not make prescriptions free.** GOV.UK says clearly that after paying the IHS you still pay for prescriptions. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-and-students-not-exempt)
- **Being a student does not automatically make prescriptions free either.** Students, like everyone else, need to check whether they meet the conditions for free or reduced-cost prescriptions. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-and-students-not-exempt)

## Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC)

If you need several prescription medicines long term, look into a **PPC**. It is not insurance: you pay an amount in advance, and while it is valid you generally don't pay item by item for NHS prescriptions in England.

The current prices are:

- 3 months: £32.05;
- 12 months: £114.50.

According to NHSBSA, a PPC may save you money if you need more than 3 prescription items in 3 months, or more than 11 in a year. If you only collect a prescription once or twice a year, it may not be worth it. Before buying, NHSBSA also suggests checking whether you are already entitled to free prescriptions. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-prepayment-certificates)

There is also an HRT PPC for hormone replacement therapy, at £19.80 for 12 months. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescription-prepayment-certificates)

## Running low on a regular medicine

It is best to get repeat prescriptions from your GP in good time, rather than waiting until your medicine runs out.

If it has already run out and you cannot reach your GP, the NHS website suggests:

- if your medicine has run out completely and you need it urgently, you can use the **emergency prescription service on 111 online**; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-running-out-of-regular-medicine)
- you can also **call 111** to discuss how to get an emergency supply until you can get your regular prescription; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-running-out-of-regular-medicine)
- pharmacies can sometimes provide certain emergency medicines without a prescription, **but you may have to pay**, and whether they supply anything, and what, is up to the pharmacist; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-running-out-of-regular-medicine)
- if it really is an emergency, go to an urgent treatment centre or A&E. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-running-out-of-regular-medicine)

## The medicines you took before moving to the UK

Many people have taken blood pressure, diabetes or other long-term medicines for years before coming to the UK. Here, ask a GP or pharmacist how to plan for your next supply.

Be prepared: no rule says a UK GP must prescribe according to a prescription issued abroad. The GP will decide using their own clinical judgement. They may ask about your situation and do some tests, then decide whether to continue a medicine with the same active ingredient, switch to a different medicine, or adjust the dose. According to GOV.UK guidance on controlled drugs, people planning to stay in the UK for more than 3 months need to get further supplies through a UK doctor. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-uk-clinician-for-continuing-supply)

So bringing the medicines is not enough on its own. It is best to bring this information as well:

- the medicine name, **ideally the generic name (the name of the active ingredient)**, not just the brand name;
- the strength of each tablet (for example, how many milligrams), how much you take each time and how many times a day;
- why you take it, i.e. the diagnosis;
- allergies;
- relevant medical records, test reports and specialist opinions.

These are not documents you are officially required to submit, but with them your GP will understand your situation much faster. If your records are in a language other than English, NHS England's guidance to practices says health documents in other languages that patients bring should, where there is a clinical need, be translated into English by a qualified translator, and where necessary both languages kept in the record. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-foreign-health-records-translation)

## Why knowing only a brand name used abroad is not enough

A medicine's brand name is chosen by the manufacturer, while the generic name is the name of its active ingredient. Different manufacturers can sell the same active ingredient under different brands.

The NHS generally prescribes by generic name unless there is a clinical reason not to. So if you tell a UK doctor a brand name used abroad, they may well not recognise it; the name of the active ingredient is much clearer. The active ingredient is usually on the box; you can take a photo, or ask the clinician who prescribed it to write the generic name on your medicine list. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-generic-prescribing)

But you cannot simply assume that "same ingredient means exactly the same". For some medicines, different brands should not be swapped freely, such as modified-release forms, some medicines with a narrow therapeutic range, devices like inhalers and insulin pens, and biological medicines. A medicine supplied abroad may also not have an approved equivalent in the UK. Which one to use is for a UK doctor to decide. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-brand-prescribing-exceptions)

## Can you bring medicines into the UK?

First, one thing to be clear about: the commonly quoted online rule that "you can only bring 3 months' supply" is, in the official rules we found, only for **controlled drugs**. For ordinary medicines that are not controlled drugs, we have not found any official overall limit on quantity. For these, GOV.UK only says to check the import rules of the MHRA (the UK medicines regulator). So we do not give a specific number here; it is safest to bring what you personally need, in the original packaging, with a prescription or a medicine list written by a doctor. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-non-controlled-medicine-import)

For controlled drugs, the GOV.UK rules are: [See the official source](#guide-evidence-controlled-drugs-import-rules)

- you can carry at most **3 months'** supply into the UK, and it must have been lawfully prescribed to you in the country where you normally live;
- you need a letter from your doctor proving the medicine was prescribed for you, with your name, travel dates, a list of medicines with doses and strengths, signed by the prescriber;
- more than 3 months' supply, or supplies posted later, will be seized; if you have a special need to bring more, you can apply for a personal licence in advance;
- some of the most tightly controlled drugs (Schedule 1) cannot be brought in under any circumstances without a licence.

To find out whether your medicine is a controlled drug, ask the prescribing doctor or check the guidance on GOV.UK.

## Herbal and traditional medicines

Check ingredients and any restrictions for herbal or traditional products too:

- the MHRA has said that most herbal products on the UK market are unlicensed, and has warned that some herbal products were found to contain toxic aristolochia, heavy metals or undeclared pharmaceutical ingredients. When buying herbal products in the UK, look for a THR or PL number on the packaging, which shows the product has been assessed by the MHRA; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-herbal-products-and-imports)
- medicines containing ingredients from endangered species may need a CITES permit to enter the UK, and cannot be brought in freely; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-herbal-products-and-imports)
- bringing meat and dairy products for personal use from most non-EU countries is not allowed; check carefully before bringing products containing animal ingredients. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-herbal-products-and-imports)

Also, if you take a herbal or traditional medicine, it is best to tell your GP when you see them.

## Why won't UK doctors prescribe antibiotics?

If you took antibiotics in similar situations before, it may seem strange when a GP or pharmacist in the UK does not give them for the same symptoms.

The NHS explains that antibiotics do not work for viral infections, such as colds, flu and most coughs, and that taking antibiotics when you don't need them can mean they may not work when you really do. So UK doctors and pharmacists first judge whether antibiotics are really needed, and will not prescribe them just because you took them in similar situations before. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-antibiotics-not-for-viral-infections)

Whether you need antibiotics is for the doctor or pharmacist seeing you to decide, based on your situation.

## What to prepare when you first arrive

- For each medicine you take: generic name, strength, dose, how many times a day, and why you take it;
- allergies and main medical history, ideally with a short English summary of your overseas records;
- medicines you bring in their original packaging, with a prescription or medicine list; for controlled drugs, a doctor's letter as required by GOV.UK;
- register with a GP as early as possible and, if you take regular medicines, book a GP appointment before the medicines you brought run out;
- remember: if your medicine is running out and you can't reach your GP, use the emergency prescription service on 111 online, or call 111.
